---
title: Running other languages with Jupyter kernels
---

## Overview

The [Jupyter engine](engines.qmd) runs code cells on a **Jupyter kernel**.
Python is only one of many: any language with an installed kernel works, so a
`{ggsql}`, `{julia}` or `{r}` cell runs the same way a `{python}` cell does.
This page uses [ggsql](https://ggsql.org) as the worked example, then explains
how Quarto picks the kernel and what it does when none is installed.

You need a `jupyter` executable on your `PATH`. Quarto checks for it by
running `jupyter --version`; without it the Jupyter engine is unavailable.

## Worked example: ggsql

Install Jupyter and the ggsql kernel into a virtual environment, then register
the kernel. Activate the environment first: `ggsql-jupyter --install` runs
`jupyter kernelspec install`, so `jupyter` has to be on your `PATH`.

```bash
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install jupyter ggsql-jupyter
ggsql-jupyter --install
```

`jupyter kernelspec list` shows the kernels Quarto can see; it should list
`ggsql`. Run Quarto from a shell where that environment is still active, so
that its `jupyter` is the one Quarto finds.

A document with a `{ggsql}` cell then needs no engine configuration at all:

````{.markdown filename="penguins.qmd"}
---
title: Penguins
format: html
---

```{ggsql}
VISUALISE species AS fill
FROM ggsql:penguins
DRAW bar
```
````

```bash
q2 render penguins.qmd
```

Quarto sees that no other engine claims `ggsql`, gives the cell to Jupyter,
and finds the kernel whose `language` is `ggsql`. The plot appears in the
output. Neither an `engine:` key nor a `jupyter:` key is needed.

::: {.callout-note}
Cell options written as `#|` comments in a `{ggsql}` cell have not been
tested. ggsql's own comment syntax is `--`.
:::

## How Quarto picks the kernel

Quarto uses one kernel for the whole document. It picks it in this order:

1. **The `jupyter:` key** in the document's front matter. Write a kernel name,
   or a map with a `kernel` entry:

   ```yaml
   jupyter: ggsql
   ```

   ```yaml
   jupyter:
     kernel: ggsql
   ```

2. **The engine configuration**, `engine: [{jupyter: {kernel: ggsql}}]`
   (see [engine configuration](engines.qmd)).
3. **The language of the cells.** Quarto looks for the first installed kernel
   whose `language` matches the first executable cell's language, ignoring
   case. For Python, a kernel inside the active virtual environment is
   preferred.

A `jupyter:` map without a `kernel` entry, and Quarto 1's `kernelspec:`
object, name no kernel. Quarto warns ([`Q-18-4`](../../errors/engine/Q-18-4.qmd))
and falls back to the next rule.

Once a kernel is picked, **every cell Jupyter owns runs on it**, whatever the
cell's language. This differs from Quarto 1, which ran only the cells written
in the kernel's own language.

### Inline expressions

The `jupyter:` key also makes a document that holds only inline expressions
run: the key selects the kernel, and spans written in that kernel's language
run on it. The key has to be in the document's own front matter. A
project-level `jupyter:` picks the kernel for pages that have cells, but does
not make a page without cells start the engine. See
[Inline expressions](computations.qmd#inline-expressions) for where spans are
and are not evaluated.

## Which cells run

Jupyter runs the cells in the languages it owns. When no engine claims a
language, Jupyter owns it, so `ggsql` or any other language with a kernel runs
without a list of supported languages anywhere. Two cases leave a cell alone:

- another engine owns its language (a `{r}` cell under `engine: knitr`), or
- you named an `engine:` that does not cover the language: your list is the
  complete statement of who runs what.

Such cells stay in the output as written.

### Fence aliases

Quarto 2 accepted a few short fence names, `py`, `jl`, `rs`, `rb`, `ts` and
`js`. They are deprecated, and a warning says so; they will be removed. Write
`python`, `julia`, `rust`, `ruby`, `typescript` and `javascript`.

## When no kernel is installed

If Jupyter owns a language but no installed kernel declares it,
[`Q-18-5`](../../errors/engine/Q-18-5.qmd) reports it:

- In a document without an `engine:` list, it is a **warning**. The cell is
  left as written and is not run, and the render continues.
- In a document with an `engine:` list, it is an **error**, and the render
  stops before any cell runs.

Either way the fix is to install a kernel for the language, then check
`jupyter kernelspec list`. If the cell is only meant to be shown, give it
`eval: false`. A document that names its kernel with `jupyter:` is not checked
against the installed kernels: every cell goes to the kernel you named.

## Mixed-language documents with SoS

Quarto runs a document on one kernel, so a document that mixes `{python}` and
`{ggsql}` cells needs a kernel that can run both. The
[SoS](https://vatlab.github.io/sos-docs/) kernel is such a multiplexing
kernel. Select it with `jupyter:`, and switch language inside a cell with a
`%use` line:

````{.markdown filename="mixed.qmd"}
---
jupyter: sos
---

```{python}
x = 21
print(x * 2)
```

```{ggsql}
%use ggsql
VISUALISE species AS fill
FROM ggsql:penguins
DRAW bar
```

```{python}
%use sos
print(x + 1)
```
````

Because every cell runs on the one SoS kernel, a `{python}` fence goes to SoS
like any other, which is why the last cell needs `%use sos` after the ggsql
cell switched the subkernel. SoS prints the ggsql subkernel's log lines in the
cell's output. Quarto does not choose SoS's subkernel from the fence language, and
fences without `%use` lines in a mixed document have not been tested.
